lesson.title: Can I Do This? The Belief That Shapes Whether You Try
lesson.summary: Self-efficacy is a person's belief in their own capability to succeed at a specific task, and Bandura identified four sources that build or undermine it, including the observational learning covered in the previous chapters.
lesson.body:
Social learning theory and observational learning explain how people acquire behaviors by watching others. Bandura used that same framework to explain something more internal: why some people persist through difficulty while others give up, even when they have similar skills. His answer centered on self-efficacy, a person's belief in their own capacity to successfully carry out the actions needed to achieve a specific goal.

Self-efficacy is often confused with self-esteem, but they are different. Self-esteem is a broad, general sense of one's own worth. Self-efficacy is narrow and situational: it's not "am I a good person" but "can I do this particular thing." Someone can have strong self-efficacy for public speaking and weak self-efficacy for calculus, entirely independent of how they feel about themselves overall.

Bandura proposed four main sources of self-efficacy. Mastery experiences, actually succeeding at a task yourself, are the strongest source, since direct personal success is hard to argue with. Vicarious experiences, watching someone similar to you succeed, is the second source, and this is where self-efficacy connects directly back to observational learning: seeing a peer struggle and eventually succeed at something can raise your own belief that you could do it too, even before you've tried. Verbal or social persuasion, encouragement and feedback from others, is a third, generally weaker but still meaningful source. And physiological or emotional states, how you interpret your own racing heart or calm nerves before a challenge, form a fourth source; interpreting that arousal as excitement versus as dread can shift efficacy in either direction.

Self-efficacy matters because it shapes behavior well before any actual ability differences come into play: it influences what goals people set in the first place, how much effort they put in, how long they persist when things get hard, and how they respond to setbacks. Two students with identical math skills but different self-efficacy beliefs will often choose different courses, put in different amounts of practice, and react very differently to a bad test grade.
